title: The Six-Week Lag: Why Christmas Trading Capital Has to Be Arranged in September, Not November
excerpt: By the time December's cash squeeze is obvious, the finance that would have covered it needed six to eight weeks lead time. Here's why that conversation has to start in September.
content:
Every year the same fortnight arrives. Stock needs to land before the Christmas rush, casual staff need rostering before trading hours extend, and wages for the busiest six weeks of the year all fall due before the season's revenue has actually landed in the account. For a lot of owner-led businesses across retail, hospitality and trade, this is the heaviest cash outlay of the entire year, arriving well ahead of the cash it's meant to generate.

The instinct, understandably, is to deal with it when it becomes a problem. Trading ramps up through November, the gap between outgoings and incomings shows up in the bank balance, and only then does the thought arise that the existing overdraft or facility might not stretch far enough to cover it. That is usually the moment the finance conversation starts, and it is already too late to start it well.

A genuine increase to a working capital facility, a new overdraft limit or a short-term seasonal line rarely moves in days. Between updated financials, a credit assessment, a security review and internal sign-off, six to eight weeks between a first conversation and funds actually being available is a realistic timeline at most Australian lenders. Applied in November, that timeline lands somewhere in the second week of January, well after the trading peak it was meant to fund.

Why the Gap Feels Sudden but Isn't

The Christmas cash squeeze rarely arrives out of nowhere. It's the predictable outcome of a calendar most retail, hospitality and trade businesses already know well, a business trading through the Gold Coast's summer peak feels this as clearly as anyone: stock or staffing costs load up from October, revenue follows from mid-December, and the gap between the two is the same gap every year, just easy to underestimate until the invoices are actually due. What changes isn't whether the gap exists. It's whether anyone modelled its size early enough to do something about it.

What a Lender Actually Wants to See

Approving extra working capital, whatever form it takes, comes down to the same handful of questions for most business lenders: what does the cash flow actually look like over the specific weeks in question, what security sits behind the request, and does the trading history support the seasonal pattern being described. A business that arrives with a clear weekly cash flow forecast covering the actual peak, rather than a general request for more headroom, moves through that assessment considerably faster than one asking a lender to take the pattern on faith.

This is also where an existing facility gets tested against reality rather than assumption. Plenty of businesses carry an overdraft limit that was adequate two Christmases ago and have never checked whether it still covers a business that has grown since. A banking and facility review answers that question directly, comparing the current facility against what the actual trading peak requires and flagging the gap while there is still time to close it, rather than discovering the shortfall from an overdrawn account in the second week of December.

The Cost of Leaving It to November

Running it reactively rarely means the finance never arrives. More often it means it arrives on worse terms, structured as an emergency overdraft extension at a higher rate than a properly negotiated facility would have carried, or it means a stock order gets trimmed to fit the cash available rather than the demand actually expected. Either way, the cost of the delay lands during the exact weeks the business is meant to be making its year. None of that is a failure of judgement. It's simply what happens when a genuinely seasonal, predictable need gets treated as an unexpected one.

The Conversation Worth Having in September

The businesses that get ahead of this aren't doing anything complicated. They build a short cash flow forecast for the specific peak weeks, check that against what the current facility can actually absorb, and have the lender conversation, if one is needed, while trading is still calm enough to negotiate properly rather than settle for whatever is available quickly. Six weeks before the pressure hits is a considered conversation. Six weeks after is damage control.

None of this requires a large business or a finance team to do properly, it just requires doing it before the calendar forces the issue. If the current facility hasn't been tested against this year's Christmas trading peak, or the forecast for those six weeks has never actually been built, now is the window to do both. Book a discovery call and have the numbers ready well before November makes the decision for you.

faqs.q: How many weeks in advance should Christmas trading finance be arranged?
faqs.a: Most Australian lenders need six to eight weeks between an initial conversation and funds being available, once financials, security and internal sign-off are accounted for. Applied in November, that timeline lands well into January, after the trading peak it was meant to cover. September or early October gives a business genuine room to negotiate properly rather than accept whatever is available quickly.

faqs.q: What does a bank need to approve extra working capital for the Christmas period?
faqs.a: Lenders generally want three things: a clear cash flow forecast covering the specific peak weeks, the security available against the request, and trading history that supports the seasonal pattern being described. A 13-Week Cash Flow Build mapped against the actual peak moves an application through assessment considerably faster than a general request for more headroom.

faqs.q: Will my existing overdraft automatically cover a busier Christmas trading period?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, and this is one of the more common gaps. An overdraft limit set two or three Christmases ago was sized for the business as it existed then, not the one trading now. It's worth checking the current limit against this year's forecast peak rather than assuming last year's headroom still applies.

faqs.q: What does a banking and facility review actually involve for an SME?
faqs.a: It's an independent check of the facilities already in place against what the business's current trading actually requires, including whether the limit, security and pricing still fit. Ahead of a seasonal peak, a banking and facility review is worth doing well before the cash gap appears, since a shortfall found in September can still be fixed, while one found in December usually can't.

faqs.q: Is asset or stock finance faster to arrange than an overdraft increase?
faqs.a: It depends on the lender and the security involved, but neither moves quickly if it starts as an emergency request. Both still require updated financials, an assessment of the asset or stock being financed, and internal approval, so the real advantage comes from starting the process early rather than from choosing one instrument over the other.

faqs.q: How does a fractional CFO help prepare a business for a seasonal finance application?
faqs.a: A fractional CFO typically builds the weekly cash flow forecast a lender actually wants to see, tests it against the existing facility, and packages the numbers into a case a bank can assess quickly. That preparation is usually the difference between a straightforward approval and a drawn-out back and forth during the exact weeks a business can least afford the delay.
